title: 98 Years of the Stock Market: Every Crash, Every Recovery – How Long Can It Keep Going Up?
title_card: How long can the stock market keep going up?
description: $100 put into the 500 biggest US companies in 1928 grew to about $1.16 million by 2025 – through the Great Depression, 1974, 2008 and 2022. We go through 98 years of real data: how often the market falls, the worst crashes, how long recoveries took once you count inflation, and what history says about 1, 10 and 20-year periods. History, not a prediction, and not advice.
tags: how long can the stock market go up
sources: Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern School of Business, 'Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds, Bills and Real Estate: 1928–2025' (histretSP.xls): annual S&P 500 total returns including dividends, nominal and real, and US inflation (CPI-U, from FRED), 1928–2025

Own calculations from that dataset: value of $100 invested at the start of 1928 (nominal and real), year-end declines from a previous high and the year a new high was reached, share of rolling 1-, 5-, 10-, 15- and 20-year periods with a positive real return, compound annual growth rates
Past returns do not predict future returns; figures use year-end values, so declines within a year were deeper than shown

beats.say: A hundred dollars. Put into the five hundred biggest American companies at the start of 1928 – with every dividend reinvested.
By the end of 2025, it would be worth about one point one six million dollars.
And in between: the Great Depression, a world war, the oil crisis, the dot-com crash, 2008, a pandemic.
So how long can this keep going up? Nobody knows the future. But we do have ninety-eight years of data. Let's look at every crash, and how long it really took to recover – after inflation.

show.source: S&P 500 total returns 1928–2025 · Damodaran, NYU Stern

beats.say: Quick note: this is general information, not financial advice.
Start with the simplest question: how often does the market go up in a year?
In seventy-two of ninety-eight years, US stocks ended the year higher. About three years out of four.
Which means in about one year out of four, they ended lower. Twenty-six down years. Losing years aren't rare accidents. They're part of the deal.
Here's the whole journey, on a special scale where every step up the chart means the money multiplied by ten.

show.heading: $100 in US stocks in 1928
show.sub: Before inflation, log scale · S&P 500 incl. dividends, year ends · Damodaran, NYU Stern

beats.say: From a hundred dollars to about a thousand by 1955. Past ten thousand in 1983. About a hundred and fifty-seven thousand at the end of 1999.
And past a million in 2025. On average, almost exactly ten percent a year.
But ten percent is an average of very different years. The best year was 1954: plus fifty-three percent. The worst: minus forty-four percent. Almost never does a single year look like the average.
Now the painful part. Here are the seven worst years since 1928.

show.heading: The worst years for US stocks since 1928: loss in %
show.source: S&P 500 incl. dividends, year ends · Damodaran, NYU Stern

beats.say: 1931, in the middle of the Great Depression: minus forty-four percent in one year. And that was the third losing year in a row.
2008, the financial crisis: minus thirty-seven percent.
1974, the oil crisis, with inflation above twelve percent: minus twenty-six.
2002, the end of the dot-com bubble: minus twenty-two – also the third losing year in a row. And 2022, the most recent one: minus eighteen percent.
Notice something else: the worst years cluster. 1930 and 1931 came back to back. So did 1973 and 1974, and 2000 to 2002. When it goes wrong, it often goes wrong for a while.

These are year-end numbers. Inside those years, it was often worse. And look at 2020: the pandemic crash came in the spring – and the year still ended up eighteen percent. Crashes and recoveries can happen in the same few months.
Every one of these felt, at the time, like it might be the end. That's what makes them hard: you never see the recovery from inside the crash.
Now the question that matters: how long did it take to get back? And here's where most charts lie to you – they ignore inflation.

show.heading: $100 in US stocks in 1928, after inflation
show.sub: In 1928 dollars, log scale · S&P 500 incl. dividends, year ends · Damodaran, NYU Stern

beats.say: This is the same hundred dollars, but measured in 1928 dollars – what it could actually buy. Prices rose about nineteen-fold since 1928, so this is the honest line.
The Great Depression: from the end of 1928 to the end of 1931, real value fell by fifty-five percent. With prices falling too, it was back above the old high at the end of 1936.
Now the one people forget: the 1970s. From 1972 to 1974, the real value fell forty-eight percent. Not only because stocks fell – inflation ate the rest.
And it took until 1984 to get back. Ten years of waiting, in real money.
The longest wait of all came recently. The real high at the end of 1999 – then the dot-com crash, then 2008. At the bottom, minus forty-two percent.
Back above the 1999 high only at the end of 2013. Fourteen years, for someone who put money in at the very top.
And 2022: minus twenty-three percent after inflation, recovered by the end of 2024.
So the honest answer: recoveries have taken anywhere from two years to fourteen. And nobody rang a bell at the bottom.

show.caption: time to a new real high after big crashes

beats.say: So let's take the unluckiest person in modern market history. Say Mark puts ten thousand dollars into the S&P 500 on the last day of 1999. The exact top before the dot-com crash.

show.caption: invested at the end of 1999 – the top

beats.say: Three years later, after three losing years in a row, his ten thousand is worth about six thousand two hundred and fifty. He's down more than a third.
Then 2008 hits. Nine years in, his ten thousand dollars is worth about seventy-two hundred. Still below where he started. Most people would have sold here – and a lot of people did.
But Mark does nothing. By the end of 2025, his ten thousand dollars is worth about seventy-four thousand – before inflation.

After inflation, it's still about three point eight times the buying power he started with. The worst possible entry point of the last thirty years – and still a multiple, if he waited twenty-six years.

Now compare Lisa, who invested the same ten thousand at the end of 2002, near the bottom. She ends with about a hundred and eighteen thousand. Perfect timing beat terrible timing by a lot – but nobody could know in 2002 that it was the bottom.
The real risk for Mark was never the crash itself. It was selling in the middle of it, and missing the way back.
Now the chart that changes how most people see the market. Instead of single years, take every possible period since 1928 – every one-year stretch, every five-year stretch, and so on.

show.heading: Share of periods that beat inflation
show.source: Every rolling period 1928–2025 · S&P 500 incl. dividends, year ends · Damodaran, NYU Stern

beats.say: Over any single year, stocks beat inflation sixty-eight percent of the time. Roughly a coin flip with a bit of luck on your side.
Over five years: seventy-seven percent. Over ten years: eighty-eight percent. Over fifteen: ninety-four.
And over twenty years? Every single twenty-year period from 1928 to 2025 – seventy-nine of them – ended with more buying power than it started with.
Even the worst one – starting at the end of 1928, right before the Depression – still grew a little faster than prices: about six tenths of a percent a year after inflation.
The worst ten-year stretch, though – 1999 to 2008 – lost almost four percent a year after inflation. Ten years is not as long as it sounds.
If this already changed how you see a market crash, leave a like – it really helps the channel.

chapters.heading: So how long can it go up?

beats.say: Back to the question: how long can the stock market keep going up? The honest answer has two halves.

show.text: Short term: *anything* can happen. Long term: it has always recovered – so far.
show.source: US stocks 1928–2025 · history is not a guarantee

beats.say: Half one: in any given year, the market can fall a lot. Twenty-six times in ninety-eight years it did. And after the crash, the wait can be long – fourteen years, in real terms, after 1999.

Half two: over long stretches, it has always come back – because the price of a company follows what it earns. When businesses earn more over time, their value grows with them, and dividends get paid along the way.
After inflation, a hundred dollars from 1928 grew to about sixty-one thousand in 1928 dollars. That's about six point eight percent a year, in real buying power.

show.caption: average real return a year, US stocks 1928–2025

beats.say: But that's one country, the US – which had one of the best centuries of any stock market. Other markets did worse. And the next ninety-eight years can look different. History shows what was possible. It doesn't promise it.
What history does show clearly: the people who got the average weren't the ones who timed it. They were the ones who were still there when the recovery came.
So, three things from ninety-eight years of data.

show.heading: $100 in US stocks in 1928, after inflation
show.sub: In 1928 dollars, log scale · S&P 500 incl. dividends, year ends · Damodaran, NYU Stern

beats.say: One: crashes are normal. US stocks fell in about one year out of four, and seven times by eighteen percent or more.
Two: count inflation. After the seventies and after 1999, it took ten and fourteen years to get the buying power back – longer than most charts show.
Three: time changed the odds. Over one year, stocks beat inflation about two times in three. Over every twenty-year period since 1928, they did every time. History, not a promise.
If you want to understand your money with real numbers, subscribe. Next time, we'll do the math on what a few hundred dollars a month can become.
A hundred dollars in the five hundred biggest US companies in 1928, dividends reinvested, became about one point one six million dollars by 2025.
But it was never a smooth ride. Stocks fell in twenty-six of those ninety-eight years. Minus forty-four percent in 1931. Minus thirty-seven in 2008.

show.heading: The worst years for US stocks since 1928: loss in %
show.source: S&P 500 incl. dividends, year ends · Damodaran, NYU Stern

beats.say: Count inflation, and the waits get long. After the top at the end of 1999, it took until 2013 to get the buying power back. Fourteen years of waiting.

show.heading: $100 in US stocks in 1928, after inflation
show.sub: In 1928 dollars, log scale · S&P 500 incl. dividends, year ends · Damodaran, NYU Stern

beats.say: And yet: every single twenty-year period since 1928 ended with more buying power than it started with. Seventy-nine out of seventy-nine. History, not a promise.

Someone who put ten thousand dollars in at the very top in 1999 – the worst timing of the last thirty years – still had about seventy-four thousand by the end of 2025, before inflation. Every crash and every recovery is in the full video on the channel.
